summary: Rabbi Shimon says a married woman may not sell property her husband knows about, and if she does it does not count. Property he does not know about she also should not sell, but if she does, it counts.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon makes a difference between kinds of property.
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between one type of property and another type of property:

chunks.en: Property that the husband knows about,

chunks.en: she may not sell.

chunks.en: And if she sold it or gave it away,

chunks.st: the transaction is void. Property that is unknown to the husband

chunks.en: she may not sell,
chunks.st: she may not sell,

chunks.en: but if she sold it or gave it away, it counts.
chunks.st: but if she sold it or gave it away, the transaction is valid.

summary: Rabbi Shimon says that what the husband gains when the marriage starts, he loses when it ends, and the other way around. He shows this with fruit attached to the ground and fruit already picked.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: Where he has the better side when she comes in,
chunks.st: In a case where his right is superior upon her entrance to the marriage,

chunks.en: he has the worse side when she leaves.
chunks.st: his right is inferior upon her exit if he divorces her.

chunks.en: Where he has the worse side when she comes in,
chunks.st: Conversely, in a case where his right is inferior upon her entrance,

chunks.en: he has the better side when she leaves.
chunks.st: his right is superior upon her exit.

chunks.en: Fruit attached to the ground:
chunks.st: How so? With regard to produce that is attached to the ground,

chunks.en: when she comes in they are his, and when she leaves they are hers.
chunks.st: if she married while owning such produce, upon her entrance it is his, in accordance with the opinion of the Rabbis, and upon her exit, when he divorces her, it is hers, as it is considered part of her property.

chunks.en: And fruit picked from the ground:
chunks.st: But in the case of produce that is detached from the ground,

chunks.en: when she comes in they are hers, and when she leaves they are his.
chunks.st: upon her entrance it is hers, and if such produce is detached before their divorce, upon her exit it is his,
chunks.stMore: as he was already entitled to all the produce of her property.

summary: A widow waiting for her yavam may sell property she inherited. Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel argue about who gets her kesubah and her property if she dies.

chunks.st: As for the property that comes and goes with her,

chunks.en: stays with her father's heirs.
chunks.st: it is in the possession of the heirs of the woman’s father, as it belongs to the woman.

summary: A husband may not set aside just one pile of money for the kesubah; all his property stands behind it. If the yavam divorces her and takes her back, she gets only her kesubah.

chunks.en: rather, all of his property stands behind the kesubah.
chunks.st: Rather, all of the first husband’s property is mortgaged for her marriage contract as long as he has not divorced her.
